rules.covers: deletes and customer emails by agent tools only after a human approval call
every agent tool that emails a customer calls the approval function on every path

ask_parts_not_covered.part: agents shouldn't call tools the owner hasn't explicitly given them

ask_parts_not_covered.why: other: read as approval-gated deletes, not a ban; a ban is a one-line stack.statement_forbidden the owner can choose

ask_parts_not_covered.part: the approval is actually granted and its id is passed through

assumptions: Customer 'without a human approving it first' applies to both deletes and emails.
request_human_approval is the approval mechanism, as in the workspace's function file.
Tool objects are the agent's tools; the agent object itself carries no tool allowlist check.
db.bulk.delete and util.send_email are valid statement names for ordering checks.
stack.statement_order flags an after-statement with no preceding guard at all, not only a wrong order.
confusions: No check for an agent's tool allowlist. The catalogue's agent entries cover only naming, settings, tags, descriptions and credential literals, so the 'only tools I gave it' part of the ask has no home. The skill doesn't say this up front.

The catalogue says db.del is judged inside called functions for stack.statement_forbidden, but it's unclear whether stack.statement_order follows called functions. I assumed it doesn't, so a delete hidden in a helper would be missed.

stack.statement_order's before param says a guard must be 'ahead of each after match', but it doesn't say whether the guard has to be unconditional. That matters for approval gates, so I added AGENT-020 to cover the unconditional case separately.

Choosing between a ban (stack.statement_forbidden) and an approval gate (ordering or statement_required) for deletes wasn't spelled out. The ask said 'without approval', which pointed to the gate, but a product default would help.
The catalogue's object_kinds lists are long and contain 'tool' in several entries, so grepping it for agent-tool checks gives a lot of noise. A per-object-kind index would help.
Parsing with `xano policy parse -f` printed the reformatted file and no warnings. I couldn't tell whether a missing workspace name would show as a warning, since all names I used exist.
wished_for: An example of approval-gated deletes and emails in one policy, using request_human_approval.
A check that compares an agent's tools list against an allowlist, or a recipe for expressing one.
Clarity on whether stack.statement_order and object.statement_required follow called functions.
A template for human-in-the-loop approval requirements.
why_confidence: The approval-before-email and approval-before-delete parts map to real checks, and both files parse. Confidence is only medium because I couldn't evaluate the rules against the workspace (not allowed), the tool-allowlist half of the ask has no check, and the ordering check's handling of called functions and conditional guards is unclear from the catalogue.
